summary: Amara is eager to reconnect with her heritage through learning Yoruba but feels limited by language apps that don't offer it, using Duolingo for French instead while seeking more personalized and cultural language education.
top_quotes: I really want to learn Yoruba to feel closer to my roots, but these language apps never have it.
Duolingo is helping me with French, but I need something like that for Yoruba.
I just hope these apps can understand how important language is for connecting with culture.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey there! How you dey? I'm looking forward to our chat.

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Ah, where do I start? I was born in Nigeria but moved to Houston when I was quite young. I've been here for most of my life, but my Nigerian roots run deep. My parents always spoke Yoruba at home but, you know, growing up here, it's easy to just lose that, so now I'm really trying to reconnect with my heritage. I'm also a professional, working in IT, and I enjoy anything that keeps me learning and growing.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up mostly in Houston. My family came here when I was around 8 years old, so most of my memories are from here.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: It was quite an experience, sha. Houston is diverse, so it was nice to see lots of different cultures. But, it was also a bit of a struggle trying to balance my Nigerian identity with American life. My parents kept us rooted in our culture as much as they could, but school and everything else was very American, you know?

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Moving to the U.S. was definitely a turning point. It changed everything, really. It opened up so many opportunities, but it also meant I had to adjust to a whole new way of life and sometimes, I felt like I was leaving a part of myself behind.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Because it forced me to navigate between two cultures. It made me appreciate my Nigerian background more and instilled in me a desire to hold onto it, while also embracing this new environment. It was a constant balancing act, and it still is to some extent.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: I tried to integrate both cultures into my life as much as possible. At home, we spoke Yoruba and celebrated our traditions, while outside, I was learning and adapting to the American lifestyle. I think I learned to appreciate diversity early on because of that.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, I'm really focused on reconnecting with my roots. Language is a big part of it, because knowing Yoruba better will help me feel more connected to my heritage and even my family. Plus, I'm also keen on personal growth and learning new things.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: It's important because language connects us to our history and culture. It's like a bridge to past generations, you understand? And for me, it's also about being able to communicate more deeply with my family, especially the older folks who prefer speaking Yoruba.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day? I would say it's when I get to balance work with some quality time for myself. Maybe try to learn something new, catch up with a friend or family, and have some quiet time for reflection. When I feel like I've moved forward, even a little, it's a good day.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: I think it's when I feel accomplished and at peace. Like, I've ticked off my to-do list, but also had time to enjoy myself and reflect. It's that sense of balance, you know?

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I try to think things through carefully. I weigh the pros and cons and often talk to my family or close friends to get their perspective. It's important to listen to my gut feeling too, but having all the information is key.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I think I'm more of a planner. I like to have a clear idea of what I'm doing. I mean, I've learned to adapt and go with the flow when I need to, but having a plan gives me peace of mind.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: For instance, when I was planning to travel to Nigeria last year, I had everything mapped out—from the flight details to what I'd do each day. I even started prepping by brushing up on my Yoruba, though that didn't go as planned because there's no Duolingo for it, you know?

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I try to mitigate risks as much as I can. I'll often assess the situation, figure out what the worst-case scenario is, and prepare for it. But at the same time, I'm willing to take risks if the potential rewards are worth it, especially when it comes to personal growth.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: Ah, on a typical weekday, I wake up early, have my morning routine—like breakfast and a bit of reflection. Then, it's off to work where I'm in IT, handling various projects. It's usually quite busy. In the evenings, I try to squeeze in some exercise, maybe do a bit of reading or language learning on Duolingo, especially with French these days, and then relax before bed.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Work definitely takes a lot of energy, especially if there's a big project or deadline. Sometimes language learning can feel a bit draining too, especially when I'm trying to maintain motivation without a proper resource for Yoruba.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more time for learning Yoruba, honestly. It's a bit frustrating not having the right resources, and sometimes after a long day, I just don't have the energy to look through books or online materials.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Last year, it was probably time management. Juggling work, personal life, and trying to squeeze in learning Yoruba and French was a real challenge. There's just not enough hours in the day sometimes.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I had to prioritize better and be more disciplined with my schedule. Some things had to be put on the back burner. I also tried using productivity apps to help me stay organized, but it’s an ongoing process.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: I'm really close to my family, especially my siblings. And I have a tight-knit group of friends here in Houston. We've all been through a lot together, and they feel just like family too.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: They're supportive and understanding. We share a lot of laughs and also look out for each other. I can talk to them about anything, and I know they'll have my back no matter what.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, most of my time is either at work or at home. The commute between those places eats up quite a bit of time too.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Work can be a bit stressful at times, but it's also fulfilling when I get things done. At home, I feel relaxed and comfortable—it’s my sanctuary, you know? But sometimes I wish I had more flexibility to be in different environments.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: I think it's the routine. Work is demanding, but it's familiar, and home is where I can recharge and just be myself without any external pressures.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: My first call is usually to my sister. She's level-headed and gives good advice. If it's something more professional, I have a mentor I reach out to for guidance.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: There was a point last year when work was absolutely hectic, and on top of that, I felt like I wasn't making any progress with my language learning. It was like everything came down on me at once, and I just felt overwhelmed.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It knocked my confidence a bit. I felt like I was in over my head, and I started questioning whether I could really manage everything I had taken on. It was a period of doubt.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I took a step back, you know. I had to reassess and prioritize. My sister helped me break things down into manageable parts, and I set more realistic goals. Plus, I reminded myself of why I was doing it all in the first place, which helped me refocus.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Definitely taking breaks and doing something that clears my mind. Sometimes meditation or listening to music helps. Also, talking to someone who understands what I'm going through makes a big difference.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I hope to be more fluent in Yoruba and really feel that strong connection to my roots. I want to have traveled more, maybe taken some trips back to Nigeria. Professionally, it would be nice to have advanced in my career and maybe even start a family.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I want to have more time for personal projects and family. It would be great if language learning, especially for Yoruba, was more accessible. I just want a more balanced life overall.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: I mostly used textbooks and some online resources, but it felt so dry and wasn't engaging at all. For Yoruba, it was especially tough because resources are limited. I tried to speak with my family, but that wasn’t enough to really grasp the language structure.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: It was just very boring, you know? Textbooks can only take you so far, and without interactive elements or feedback, it felt like I wasn't actually learning. Plus, finding resources for Yoruba was nearly impossible.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: I remember once trying to follow a Yoruba lesson from a textbook before visiting family in Nigeria, and it was a disaster. I couldn't converse properly, and it was just frustrating, because I felt like all my preparation went to waste.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: A friend of mine mentioned it to me when I was complaining about wanting to learn another language more efficiently, so I decided to give it a shot.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: I liked that it was gamified and seemed more interactive than what I was using before. Plus, it was free, so I thought, why not? Sadly, they didn't have Yoruba, so I started with French to test the waters.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Alright, so usually I open the app in the evening, after work. I go through my daily lesson, which typically has a mix of listening, speaking, and writing tasks. They give you these little exercises, like matching phrases or translating sentences. It's quite interactive, and seeing immediate feedback is nice. They’ve got this funny owl mascot that keeps reminding you to practice, which is cute but sometimes annoying when you're busy!

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: I really appreciate the structure and consistency. Having a daily goal helps keep me motivated. Plus, the variety in exercises—like listening, speaking, and matching—is engaging and doesn’t feel as monotonous as other methods.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: The most frustrating part is definitely the lack of Yoruba. I mean, it's a bit disappointing that they're missing this key language that I really want to learn. It makes me feel like I'm not getting what I truly need from the app.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: Besides the lack of Yoruba, sometimes the phrases they teach feel irrelevant. Like, when am I really going to use 'The penguin drinks water' in a conversation? It feels like some of the content could be more practical.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: I remember I was on this streak, practicing daily, and then one day, I realized how much time I was putting into learning French phrases that didn’t seem useful. And I thought, 'what if this energy was going towards Yoruba?' It just hit me how much I’m missing out on.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, I do. I try to supplement Duolingo with online videos and forums where people speak Yoruba. It's not perfect, but at least I get some exposure to the language in a more natural context.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They provide context and cultural nuances that you just don't get from Duolingo. It's nice seeing how people actually use Yoruba in daily life, and I get a bit of the cultural flavor that you can't capture with just a language app.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: I think the worst-case scenario is that apps like Duolingo never expand to include languages like Yoruba. It would mean fewer people have access to learning their ancestral languages, and those languages might lose speakers over time.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it helps reinforce what I’ve learned and maybe teach me something new in a fun and engaging way. It should feel like constructive progress, not just mindless repetition.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: When I can recall phrases or use what I've learned in real-life situations, that's when I know it's working. If I'm improving and not just memorizing for the sake of it, then that's a win.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I'd definitely add more language options, especially African languages like Yoruba. That would be my number one request, as it would open doors for so many people reconnecting with their roots.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I'd change the emphasis to also include cultural context, not just language. Understanding the culture alongside the language would make for a richer, more meaningful learning experience.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we covered a lot, thank you. Just hoping more resources become available for people like me who want to learn their heritage languages.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Hmm, as long as it respects my privacy and is used for good, why not? Go ahead.
